analysis.one_liner: Tightens EPA and state control over water pollution and ocean-dumping permits.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in two House committees for the rest of the Congress and never received a hearing or a vote; it had one sponsor and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make federal EPA water-quality criteria the minimum standard in any state with weaker or no standards of its own. It would strengthen states' power to review and block federally permitted discharges into coastal waters, let states impose stricter ocean-dumping rules than federal ones, let EPA order polluters to stop discharging when they lack or violate a required state certification, and void an EPA regulation that allowed ocean discharges when environmental effects were uncertain. It died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, swimmers, fishermen, and anyone who drinks from or lives near waterways affected by industrial and municipal discharges. States gain a stronger hand: federal pollution criteria become the floor when their own standards are weaker, they get 60 days to review and attach conditions to ocean-discharge permits, and they can adopt tougher ocean-dumping rules than federal ones [S2][S3]. The bill also gives EPA explicit power to order a halt to discharges by a polluter who skipped or violated a required state certification [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: For any pollutant where EPA has published health-based criteria, those criteria become the presumptive standard in any state that has no standard or a weaker one, closing a loophole that let some states set lower limits [S2][S3].

States get at least 60 days to review permit applications for discharges into the territorial sea or contiguous zone, and no permit can issue unless EPA agrees to the conditions the state proposes [S2][S3].
EPA can order a person to cease all discharging activities until they obtain and comply with a required state water-quality certification, or sue them in civil court [S2][S3].
It nullifies the EPA regulation (40 CFR 125.123(c)) that permitted ocean discharges even where there was insufficient information to determine possible environmental degradation [S2][S3].
States may adopt ocean-dumping rules for waters in their jurisdiction only if they are more protective than federal ones, and federal agencies must assure compliance with those stricter rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that discharge wastewater into coastal and ocean waters — power plants, chemical and industrial plants, sewage systems, and dredge-spoil disposers — would face stricter, better-enforced limits and potentially halted operations until compliant. The cost would ultimately be borne in compliance spending by those facilities and, in part, by their customers and ratepayers [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Stricter discharge limits and the new stop-discharge enforcement order could shut down or slow permitted facilities — including sewage treatment and industrial outfalls — until they comply, with compliance costs passed to customers and ratepayers [S3].

The bill significantly shifts authority toward states and EPA over federal permitting decisions, and its requirement that EPA adopt every state's proposed conditions on ocean-discharge permits could delay projects and complicate federal water infrastructure permitting [S2][S3].

Applicants would face a stricter certification regime: a state's silence on a certification request would count as a denial, and a waiver option would be removed, giving states strong leverage over federally licensed projects [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver cleaner coastal and inland waters and stronger state and EPA oversight, at a real but ordinary cost of pollution-control spending by dischargers. Its main design risk is procedural friction: automatic denial of certifications and mandatory adoption of state conditions could delay some projects. It was a modest, focused amendment rather than a sweeping overhaul, and it never advanced far enough for its costs to be tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, divided among three subcommittees, and stayed there until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Douglas (Pete) Peterson of Florida introduced the bill on June 4, 1991; no other member cosponsored it [S1][S4].

It was referred jointly to the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee and the Public Works and Transportation Committee, then split among the Water Resources Subcommittee and the Oceanography and Fisheries subcommittees [S5].
Executive comments were requested from the Commerce Department, Interior, the Army Corps of Engineers, and EPA on June 18, 1991; that is the last recorded action [S5].
The bill received no hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 102nd Congress, which ended January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that discharge into coastal and ocean waters, since the stricter state-review and enforcement provisions never became law; existing, weaker rules remained in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal water dischargers; rules stayed weaker

for.name: Rep. Douglas (Pete) Peterson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tighten water-quality standards, state certification, and ocean-discharge oversight.

against.name: House Committee on Public Works and Transportation
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (later Transportation and Infrastructure); never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out or scheduled a markup; its Water Resources Subcommittee held it.

against.name: House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to two subcommittees, and never reported it or scheduled a markup.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or floor action ever occurred, and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors, so its partisan support was never measured.

industries.industry: Industrial and municipal water dischargers (coastal outfalls)
industries.note: The bill would subject their ocean and coastal discharges to stricter EPA criteria, mandatory state certification, and EPA stop orders for violators. Their interest in avoiding these controls runs against the public's interest in clean water. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Ocean dumping and dredge-spoil disposal operations
industries.note: States could impose rules stricter than federal dumping standards, and an EPA rule allowing dumping where environmental effects were unknown would be voided. Stricter limits on where and what can be dumped protect fisheries and beaches. [S2][S3]

States gain review-and-condition authority over ocean discharge permits, a floor of federal criteria, and certification denials that stick. Stronger state power here tracks the public interest in cleaner local waters. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Commercial and recreational fishing and coastal tourism
industries.note: Reduced ocean dumping and tighter discharge controls protect the fisheries, beaches, and water quality these industries depend on. [S2]
